## Executive Summary

This audit tested Avoca's internal search engine across 6 core capabilities using 59 realistic customer queries. **The results are grouped by where improvements are likely to help customer journeys most.**

In **36% of queries**, the customer was not shown a relevant result first — either no usable results at all or an off-topic top result. In particular, **25% of queries (15 of 59) returned no usable results**, most often because the search could not interpret everyday phrasing, map common terms to the right category, tolerate a typo, or honour an exclusion.

Among the queries that did return results, the best match appeared at **position #5** on average — past the first 3 results most customers look at — and in **47%** of them the best match wasn't in the top 3.

The most telling example: a customer searching "something cosy to wear around the house in winter" was shown **no usable results at all**, even though the store carries matching products.

## Test Results Summary

We ran **59 test queries** across multiple search capability categories. Here is the breakdown.

## Advanced Query Diagnostics

These diagnostics look beyond the single best result and evaluate the quality of the visible result set.

### Result Set Purity

**What it means:** This checks how much of the visible result set is actually relevant, not just whether one good result exists somewhere. A noisy top 5 means customers must visually filter around weak results even when search technically found a match.

**Result:** On 7 searches, the entire visible top 5 was off-topic — a full page of products the shopper has to discard. Across all searches that returned results, 77% of the top 5 were relevant on average — so most pages are clean, but the misses are total.

Evidence:
- “luxury throws” — not one of the 5 visible results matched; the shopper faces a full page to scroll past.
- “winter coat sale” — not one of the 5 visible results matched; the shopper faces a full page to scroll past.
- “woollen throws” — not one of the 5 visible results matched; the shopper faces a full page to scroll past.
- “knitwear not wool” — not one of the 5 visible results matched; the shopper faces a full page to scroll past.

**How to remedy it:** Tune ranking to demote low-relevance partial matches once a strong intent match exists. Add a top-N quality guardrail: for each important query class, require a minimum share of relevant results in the top 5, not only a good best-result position.

### Top Result Trust

**What it means:** This asks whether the first result is defensible as the best thing to show a customer. A bad #1 is the clearest search failure because it shapes the shopper's first impression.

**Result:** The first result is not reliable enough: 9 of 43 queries (21%) had a weak, partial, or clearly beaten #1 result.

Evidence:
- "luxury throws": #1 was "Almond Oil Duo Collection" (score 0.29). The first result is weakly related to the query.
- "bags not leather": #1 was "Chocolate Vintage Leather Miniwallet" (score 0.30). The first result is weakly related to the query.
- "knitwear not wool": #1 was "Old Copper Merino Wool Pocket Wrap" (score 0.31). The first result is weakly related to the query.
- "outerwear": #1 was "WR94 Lambswool Throw" (score 0.35). The first result is weakly related to the query.

**How to remedy it:** Add a stricter first-result threshold for high-intent queries. If the top result is weak and a stronger result exists lower, boost the stronger exact/category/brand match or suppress the weak partial match from rank #1.

### Attribute Drift

**What it means:** This decomposes multi-attribute queries to see which terms survive into the top results. It distinguishes right-category-but-wrong-attribute failures from total search failures. Only attributes that appear in product titles can be checked here; attributes carried in facet metadata (colour, size, gender) are assessed in the failure-mode analysis instead.

**Result:** 1 multi-attribute query showed genuine attribute drift: the product type was surfaced in the top results, but matching products for another title-observable attribute were ranked below it. Only attributes that actually appear in product titles are assessed; facet-only attributes are not guessed at.

Evidence:
- "home fragrance not candles": kept fragrance; buried below the top results: candle; not verifiable from titles: home

**How to remedy it:** Extract query attributes before ranking and give required attributes explicit weight. For brand, size, material, activity, and style terms, penalize results that match the product type but omit or contradict the attribute.

### Diversity vs Redundancy

**What it means:** This checks whether broad or exploratory queries show useful choice, or whether the top results are flooded by repeated variants. It is most useful for multi-brand or broad-catalog ecommerce, and less useful for true single-brand stores.

**Result:** The most redundant broad result set was "scarves": 9 unique product families across 10 top results.

Evidence:

- "pullover": 10 unique product families across 10 top results
- "throw blanket": 10 unique product families across 10 top results
- "purse": 10 unique product families across 10 top results

**How to remedy it:** Group color/size/variant duplicates under a product-family cap for broad queries. Keep exact product searches variant-rich, but diversify broad discovery queries across families, brands, styles, and use cases.

Product discovery is the search engine's ability to return the right products when a customer types a specific product name or browses a category. When it fails, customers either see a blank page or wade through unrelated products — both outcomes push them toward a competitor.

Customers rarely search the way a product catalogue is written. They describe what they want in everyday language — occasions, feelings, intended uses — and expect the search to keep up. When it cannot, entire product ranges become invisible to the customers most likely to buy them.

## Shopping Context

Customers often arrive with a specific occasion or mood in mind rather than a product name. Customers make spelling mistakes, especially on mobile. A well-functioning search catches these errors silently and returns the right products anyway. When it does not, a single misplaced letter turns a ready-to-buy customer into a dead end.

## Prioritized Roadmap

1. **Teach search to understand occasion, mood, and category intent — not just product keywords**
Fixes the complete retrieval failures across Language Understanding and Shopping Context, where queries like "Father's Day gift ideas", "end of year present for a teacher", "unique Irish gifts", "cosy loungewear", "bedtime wear", and "stationery" all returned zero results despite the store having dedicated category pages or clear inventory for each. The fix is to index category names, occasion labels, and common synonyms as searchable terms, and to create direct routing rules so that these queries land on the right category page rather than attempting a keyword match against product titles.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Quick Win

2. **Make the product type the anchor of every search — not a secondary signal**
Fixes the pattern across Product Discovery, Shopping Context, and Filters & Constraints where the engine matched on a colour, material, or season word and ignored the core product noun — causing Lambswool Throws to outrank jackets for "outerwear", cardigans and sweaters to bury throws for "woollen throws", socks and a soft toy to fill results for "throws grey", socks to dominate results for "winter coat sale", and a graphic T-shirt to outrank cashmere scarves for "grey accessories". The fix is to treat the head noun (the product type) as a near-mandatory match criterion, so that a result without "throw" in its title or category cannot outrank one that has it, and to apply a category-level boost that surfaces the correct product type before items sharing only a colour, material, or season word — colours like "grey" acting as a facet applied within the product-type result set, never as a standalone match.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Medium Effort

3. **Add semantic understanding for natural-language and intent-driven queries**
Fixes the complete retrieval failures in Language Understanding, where conversational queries like "something to keep my hands warm outside", "something to make my living room smell nice", "a gift that makes a house feel like a home", and "a nice gift for someone who loves cooking" all returned zero results because the engine could not map descriptive, intent-based phrasing to product categories. The fix requires a semantic search layer — either a vector/embedding model or a structured intent-classification dictionary — that translates conceptual descriptions into the relevant product categories before retrieval runs.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Major Project

4. **Honour exclusion words — "not" and "without" must filter results, not be ignored**
Fixes the Filters & Constraints failures where "gifts for her not jewellery" returned only jewellery, "knitwear not wool" returned only wool products, "bags not leather" returned almost exclusively leather bags, and "home fragrance not candles" still surfaced candle products. The engine currently treats "not" as a meaningless word; it needs to parse it as a hard exclusion filter that removes any result whose title, category, or material tag matches the excluded term before ranking begins.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Medium Effort

5. **Correct common misspellings rather than returning a blank page**
Fixes the Typo Tolerance failures where "knitwaer" (one transposed letter in "knitwear") and "Jellycat pluch" (one wrong letter in "plush") both returned zero results. The fix is to enable approximate matching so that queries with small spelling errors are automatically corrected before the search runs, and to add the most common misspellings of high-traffic brand names and category terms to a correction dictionary as an immediate safety net.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Quick Win

6. **Return only series members or close variants when a query exactly matches a product title**
Fixes the Product Discovery failure where searching the exact title "Shea Verbena Hands & Body Liquid Soap" correctly returned that product first but then padded the page with nine unrelated products — 'Palm Wild Replenishing Hand Wash', 'Geranium Hand & Body Wash', 'French Linen Water Hand Wash' — that share only a broad category keyword. When the search string is an exact match to a product title, the engine should restrict remaining results to variants and series members of that product, and return a short page rather than filling slots with unrelated items.
Impact: Moderate | Effort: Quick Win

Automated analysis of your site's structure, navigation categories, brands, and featured products to understand what your search engine should be able to find.

**2. Test Design**
Site-type-aware selection from a library of 26 test categories. Categories are chosen based on your site's commerce model to ensure the audit tests what matters most for your customers.

**3. Query Generation**
AI-generated realistic customer queries grounded in the actual products, brands, and categories found on your site — not generic templates.

**4. Result Collection**
Automated search execution collecting the top results for each test query exactly as your customers would see them.

**5. Relevance Scoring**
Each result scored on a 0.0–1.0 scale by a specialized relevance model, producing an objective measure of how well each result matches the query intent.

**6. Failure Analysis**
Each query classified by failure mode (e.g., no results, category not understood, constraint ignored, typo not handled, or relevant results buried) and assigned a severity based on customer impact — whether the search returned nothing, surfaced the wrong products, or simply ordered the right ones poorly.

**7. Report Assembly**
Findings synthesized into this actionable narrative with prioritized recommendations ordered by business impact.

roadmap_narrative:
1. **Teach search to understand occasion, mood, and category intent — not just product keywords**
Fixes the complete retrieval failures across Language Understanding and Shopping Context, where queries like "Father's Day gift ideas", "end of year present for a teacher", "unique Irish gifts", "cosy loungewear", "bedtime wear", and "stationery" all returned zero results despite the store having dedicated category pages or clear inventory for each. The fix is to index category names, occasion labels, and common synonyms as searchable terms, and to create direct routing rules so that these queries land on the right category page rather than attempting a keyword match against product titles.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Quick Win

2. **Make the product type the anchor of every search — not a secondary signal**
Fixes the pattern across Product Discovery, Shopping Context, and Filters & Constraints where the engine matched on a colour, material, or season word and ignored the core product noun — causing Lambswool Throws to outrank jackets for "outerwear", cardigans and sweaters to bury throws for "woollen throws", socks and a soft toy to fill results for "throws grey", socks to dominate results for "winter coat sale", and a graphic T-shirt to outrank cashmere scarves for "grey accessories". The fix is to treat the head noun (the product type) as a near-mandatory match criterion, so that a result without "throw" in its title or category cannot outrank one that has it, and to apply a category-level boost that surfaces the correct product type before items sharing only a colour, material, or season word — colours like "grey" acting as a facet applied within the product-type result set, never as a standalone match.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Medium Effort

3. **Add semantic understanding for natural-language and intent-driven queries**
Fixes the complete retrieval failures in Language Understanding, where conversational queries like "something to keep my hands warm outside", "something to make my living room smell nice", "a gift that makes a house feel like a home", and "a nice gift for someone who loves cooking" all returned zero results because the engine could not map descriptive, intent-based phrasing to product categories. The fix requires a semantic search layer — either a vector/embedding model or a structured intent-classification dictionary — that translates conceptual descriptions into the relevant product categories before retrieval runs.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Major Project

4. **Honour exclusion words — "not" and "without" must filter results, not be ignored**
Fixes the Filters & Constraints failures where "gifts for her not jewellery" returned only jewellery, "knitwear not wool" returned only wool products, "bags not leather" returned almost exclusively leather bags, and "home fragrance not candles" still surfaced candle products. The engine currently treats "not" as a meaningless word; it needs to parse it as a hard exclusion filter that removes any result whose title, category, or material tag matches the excluded term before ranking begins.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Medium Effort

5. **Correct common misspellings rather than returning a blank page**
Fixes the Typo Tolerance failures where "knitwaer" (one transposed letter in "knitwear") and "Jellycat pluch" (one wrong letter in "plush") both returned zero results. The fix is to enable approximate matching so that queries with small spelling errors are automatically corrected before the search runs, and to add the most common misspellings of high-traffic brand names and category terms to a correction dictionary as an immediate safety net.
Impact: Critical | Effort: Quick Win

6. **Return only series members or close variants when a query exactly matches a product title**
Fixes the Product Discovery failure where searching the exact title "Shea Verbena Hands & Body Liquid Soap" correctly returned that product first but then padded the page with nine unrelated products — 'Palm Wild Replenishing Hand Wash', 'Geranium Hand & Body Wash', 'French Linen Water Hand Wash' — that share only a broad category keyword. When the search string is an exact match to a product title, the engine should restrict remaining results to variants and series members of that product, and return a short page rather than filling slots with unrelated items.
Impact: Moderate | Effort: Quick Win
